Gian in the Goon BY JOE FORDHAM he image of a bullet-like rocketship landing in the eye of a whimsical 'Man in the Moon' - a human face protruding from a pie-like lunar surface - has long been an icon for imaginative cinema, gracing the mastheads of the European Fantastic Film Festivals Federation and the Visual Effects Society. The moon face, portrayed by music hall chanteuse Bleuette Bernon, originated in Voyages dans la lune (A Trip to the Moon), a 14minute silent fantasy produced by Georges Méliès' Star Film in 1902. Méliès - a native of Paris, and a former magician - produced A Trip to the Moon midway in his 500-film career, and personally oversaw creation of the film's elaborate hand-painted backdrops, mechanical props, stop-frame photography and miniatures, as well as performing as moon mission leader President Barbenfouillis. Audiences flocked to the film; but after exhibition in the United States, illegal copies began to circulate without any compensation to Méliès, and the filmmaker's career dwindled, leaving him to end his days in poverty, selling toys in a Paris train station. Writer and illustrator Brian Selznick used the story of Mélies' life as the basis for 1 / 30 The Invention of Hugo Cabret, a 526-page children's picture book and novel that inter-

HUGO wove text with intricate pencil drawings, historical photographs and motion picture frame enlargements to tell a fantasy tale about Hugo, an orphan boy living in the rafters of Gare Montparnasse in 1920s Paris, who uncovers a secret about the enigmatic toymaker in the train station lobby. The project captured the imagination of filmmaker Martin Scorsese, who optioned Selznick's book with producers Graham King and Tim Headington at GK Films and developed the story as an independently financed production, presented by Paramount Pictures as simply Hugo. Screenwriter John Logan's adaptation remained true to the tone of Selznick's book, focusing on Hugo (Asa Butterfield), his tentative friendship with an inquisitive young girl, Isabelle (Chloë Moretz), and her eccentric guardian, Papa Georges (Ben Kingsley). Ancillary characters included a spiteful station inspector (Sacha Baron Cohen), a wizened bookshop owner (Christopher Lee), cameos from notables of the 1920s Paris Left Bank art scene, and — in flashbacks — Hugo's deceased father (Jude Law), a poor clockmaker who instills in his son a curiosity about the origins of cinematic illusions. Many key crewmembers from Scorsese's previous productions reunited for the shoot in England, including production designer Dante Ferretti, cinematographer Robert Richardson, film editor Thelma Schoonmaker and visual effects supervisor Robert Legato. In a relatively brief preproduction period, cast and crew familiarized themselves with the film's historical backdrop. "To be frank," observed Rob Legato, "at the beginning of the project, all I knew about Méliès were the famous images from A Trip to the Moon. I was more intrigued by the story about this guy who reached the height of his career, watched 2 / 30 it all go away, and then had to find some redemption. But then, when I started to study

HUGO Mélies' films, I realized he was a stone-cold genius. Trip to the Moon would be hard to do with today's technology. When you think of all the steps it took to do those effects - winding back the film and re-exposing the negative, with no pin-registered cameras, no matte stands - it's impressive. In 1902, film didn't even have consistent perforations; that only became standard years later. Mélies had to use whatever equipment was available. He was an immensely clever characteri o evoke the playful inventiveness of Méliès' films, Scorsese planned to shoot screening of his own personal prints of the stereo classics Dial M for Murder and House of Wax. The filmmakers also met with Thierry Frémaux, director of the Lumière Institute in Paris, to review films by Méliès' peers, Auguste and Louis Lumière. "We viewed films that had been beautifully restored from 1895," recalled Legato. "The footage was perfectly steady, outrageously great-looking and looked like it had been filmed yesterday, some of it in 3D, and in coloriTo find a modern camera system robust enough to handle stereo and extensive visual effects, the production selected prototypes of Arriflex's Alexa digital camera. Stereographic specialist Vince Pace built a stereo rig using dual Alexas stacked vertically, gathering right- and left-eye perspectives by shooting through beamsplitter mirrors. While Pace developed stereo imaging techniques, the production team discussed methods for depicting the film's main location, Montparnasse Station - one of Paris' 3 / 30 six main rail terminals, which, since its renovation in 1969, no longer resembled the

Victorian-era structure depicted in Selznick's book. Dante Ferretti reconstructed the staHUGO tion in part on adjoining A and B Stages at Shepperton Studios, and housed additional sets containing a stationary locomotive, platforms and boarding area at Pinewood and Longcross Studios. Visual effects completed the environment with digital set extensions tailored to the filmmakers' needs. "Marty doesn't care for greenscreen," observed Legato. "He's familiar with the process, but he cannot stand not being able to see the complete image live on the set. So, while we were learning about 3D, I set up an electronic workflow knowing that my collaborators might not embrace the mechanics in the same way a filmmaker like Bob Zemeckis, Jim Cameron or Michael Bay might. Marty, Thelma and Bob just aren't interested in all the latest toys, so I had to find a way to help them accept the technology." Previsualization supervisors Nic Hatch and Martin Chamney, co-founders of Nvizage, joined the production to develop 3D animatics of virtual set extensions, initially focusing on a chase scene that follows Hugo as he flees through the crowded train station pursued by the station inspector and a dog. The main station set at Shepperton was only the middle concourse," said Martin Chamney. "We had to figure out what was beyond the greenscreen. Supervising art director Dave Warren gave us photographs of various Paris stations, and we built a hybrid design from those. The station set had architecture similar to Gare du Nord, with three practical tracks, but the platforms were narrowed down to fit in the stage. We worked with Dave Warren to develop designs for the glass roof and how we'd see through to other parts of the station to give the environment a more volu4 / 30 minous feel."

Rob could then operate the OConnor head and manipulate the previz, feeling the way the shot should move, rather than having an animator program the shot. It ensured the compositions and camera moves were very real, and achievablei For camera motion beyond the range of the OConnor head, special effects supervisor Joss Williams and his team engineered a miniature aluminum crane rigged with potentiometers that hooked into the previz system. Then Rob operated the shots. We recorded the scene with the inspector and the dog chasing Hugo in one morning, and streamed the data live into Rob's Avid so he could edit the sequencei For the main shoot, Nvizage hard-wired Ncam to motion encoders on camera rigs on set, allowing playback of set extensions in real time.iWhen we panned and tilted the camera," said Rob Legato, "Marty could see the backgrounds move in real time. HUGO incredibly bright guy, so if he saw the previz once, he got it and he could turn off the monitor. But any time we were looking in a direction we hadn't seen before, where the background was important, he would preview it live on set. It was pretty extreme to use all that technology to make a movie that felt so much like the time frame of the 1920s, but all of the devices we were using - the Alexa, previz and 3D - just melted away when we were watching the movie. That was the hook: to use the technology to our creative advantage, as opposed to steering us into a technical morass that was clever but didn't have any soul.i o depict Hugo's home within the station walls, where the young boy maintains the mechanisms of the station's 27 clocks, the special effects team rigged extensive mechanical effects to produce large-scale working machinery.iWe built the hanging clock in the station that Hugo and Isabelle clamber about in from scratchi recalled Joss Williams. "It had real working parts, no CG. That was about eight feet square. We built all the mechanisms and hung it up 18 feet for establishing shots. When the kids were inside, it was six feet off the ground, surrounded by greenscreen. The art department supplied us with drawings of how all the gears had to mesh. One of my guys, Mark Holdcroft, drew up the mechanics in Solidworks to make sure everything meshed. With Dante's approval, I added pieces that weren't on the drawings to make it look more interesting. And we built it up from there." Williams' team used high-pressure water jets to cut clock gears from aluminum, 6 / 30| made brass-plated metal parts, and then fit it with four electric motors, each of which

HUGO was rigged with electronic safety trips.iThe youngsters were in where the gears were meshing," related Williams, "so we had everything rigged on emergency e-stops. Two three-foot-tall columns sent out an infrared screen; and if anyone broke that screen, it shut down the mechanisms immediately." The largest station clock was situated in a tower atop the station that Hugo scales to evade the station inspector. '¿The Tower Clock was two stories high and as big as a house," Williams remarked. "The art department built that on C Stage at Pinewood Studios, and we made it work. Some of the cogs were four meters in diameter. We water-cut those out of fire-grade medium-density fiberboard. Bob Richardson used a large amount of light on his interiors, so it got intensely hot and we had to zinc-coat the cogs to protect them, and then we painted them to look like brass. We broke down the mechanism into four sections, each of which had its own e-stop, with a technician watching that area, and we made the teeth of any cogs Asa came into contact with out of rubberi Practical atmospheric effects also factored into the film's stereo design. Bob Richardson wanted to fill the frame with steam and other particles so the environment would appear to be coming at the viewers," said Williams. "Bob particularly wanted a lot of 'particulates' in the air, and we racked our brains to find something that would be tiny and float, but safe." The effects team devised a concoction of goose and duck down. "We went to a department store and bought all their feather pillows; and then I started up a cottage industry with my mother and sister trimming down the feathers. They did that by stuffing feathers through the end of a toilet roll and trimming them using hairdressing 7 / 30 scissors. One three-foot-by-two-foot box of cut Siberian duck and goose down particulate

HUGO took about three weeks to trim fine enough for our use. That went on for months, and my mother made a fortune." Effects technicians filled sieves above the sets with the feather particles, and used small electric motors to drop them into downdrafts created by electric fans. On the stage floor, Williams' team used manual shaker sieves and wafters to apply particulate in the foreground, and layered steam around the sets. "We used a strata misting technique we had learned on Sleepy Hollow," Williams related. "We attached a 20-foot piece of convoluted tube to the smoke machine, and then stuck a swimming pool pole on the end of that. We could then extend the smoke outlet to about 18 feet; and because of the mixture of fluids that we used, heated at different temperatures, the smoke hung in layers. he theatrical approach to depicting Hugo's world extended to views of the surthey were enhanced," observed Rob Legato. "Marty's vision of the film was photoreal - it was certainly not 'storybook' - but it was not the gritty photorealism of Goodfellas or Raging Bull, either. We wanted it to feel like Paris built on a backlot in the 1930s. It was an idealized version of the city - a love letter to the beginnings of moviesi Legato sought a visual effects vendor capable of interpreting the film's stylization while realizing an estimated 850 visual effects shots on a relatively limited independent budget. Added to the equation, Legato was aware from previous projects with Scorsese that visual effects vendors had to be open to revisions without levying automatic financial 8 / 30 penalties.iMarty's approach to visual effects is no different than changing a cut in the

HUGO edit," said Legato. "On most films, you have to turn over scenes early and not change them; and if you change them, you have to pay for it. That is very limiting for a filmmaker like Marty. And so we had to find a vendor familiar with that style. Pixomondo joined the production just before principal photography and, as the project progressed, divided up the work among 10 of its 11 international studios.iBreaking up the work was better for us and for the movie," said Pixomondo visual effects supervisor Ben Grossmann. 'It allowed us to have smaller teams with better-quality artists, rather than pouring everything into one location with 400 artists. Each studio could handle an entire sequence from start to finish, and each had its own specialty. Pixomondo Berlin is good at effects, for example, so we sent that style of scene to them. Each facility had something that they were best at, and we leveraged that." Working with digital effects supervisor Alex Henning out of Pixomondo's London studio, Grossmann first focused on creating a detailed train station, referencing Nvizage previz, art department foam-core mockups and Google SketchUp models. Pixomondo art directors Rick Rische and Ingo Putze worked in the art department to help conceptualize set extensions. We built the station architecture in homage to the old Gare Montparnasse. The back of the train station had little bits of Gare Saint-Lazarre, and at various points we used reference from the Musee d'Orsay - the former Orsay train station, which is now an art museum. We took the clock from there, for example. It was a collage of all the famous Paris train stations. For the surrounding city, Pixomondo studied archival photographs of Paris by Eugène Atget and Henri Cartier-Bresson, as well as period filmmakers - from the Lumières to 9 / 30 Charles Chaplin and René Clair - who were Scorsese's cinematic references for the film.

HUGO To gather textures for set extensions, Pixomondo shot panoramic stills in Paris using a GigaPan motion control camera mount. 'The GigaPan allows a DSLR to shoot stitched tiles up to 200,000 pixels wide," said Grossmann. "We programmed it to shoot high dynamic range bracketed exposures, 360 degrees by 90 degrees, and visited everywhere that Dante suggested. We shot everywhere from the rooftops of the Clauzel district to Montmartre, Sacred Heart cathedral, Notre Dame, the banks of the Seine, and dark and dingy alleyways in old abandoned parts of town." Layouts modified cityscapes to dramatic effect. "In our London studio, we had several French artists," said Alex Henning. "They had to come to grips with the fact that the Eiffel Tower moved about a lot. We adopted a modular approach to the city, swapping things around very much as early filmmakers might have moved façades around on a set to suit the compositioni ixomondo grouped city structures by architectural style, and modeled the staP geometric detail the closer the station was to camera," said Henning. "Up front, we had high-rez buildings that we could light very dynamically. Further back, where all we saw was a glimpse of rooftop, we were more economical with the CG. We rendered distant buildings as cubes. The stereo nature of the project dictated that we use geometry much further back than we would have if this had been a non-3D showi For an opening aerial shot descending over the city, Pixomondo produced concept 10 / 30 paintings and then blocked out the environment, focusing detail as the shot progressed

HUGO over several thousand frames to swoop down into the station, skimming the bustling concourse and ending on a closeup of Hugo behind the giant station clock. The shot set the tone for the style of camerawork in the film. Marty wanted to use a camera platform that would allow us to actually shoot that opening shot," said Rob Legato. "I started previzing with Nvizage using the mini-crane rig, framing the shot to include the Eiffel Tower, because that was such an identifiable landmark. It started as a helicopter-style move, but we opted to do that in the computer because the city was so stylized; and it was snowing, so there was no way to do that practically. The rest, inside the station, we shot as bite-sized chunks of live-actioni Working with key grip Chris Centrella, the production staged the camera's entry into the set at Shepperton on a pickup truck that drove out of a tented enclosure outside the soundstage. The camera vehicle then accelerated to a speed dictated by the previz and drove through a crowd of extras, with stunt performers closest to camera dodging out of the way. The shot continued as a motion control crane move, achieved with motion control supervisor lan Menzies at Mark Roberts Motion Control, that closed in on the station clock where Hugo's eye peers out from behind a numeral. Motion control was the only way we could get it to feel like it was all one camera move in to Asa Butterfield's eye," explained Legato. iWe shot that slower than real time, so we could re-project the texture onto geometry in 3D, and then we re-created our own camera move digitally. Hugo's image was mapped onto geometry, which gave us the ability to control the speed of the move, blending with the earlier part of the shot and making the two parts match perfectly I1 / 30 in stereo."

HUGO To ensure precision in aligning set extensions in stereo perspectives, Pixomondo surveyed each camera setup using Totalstation data correlated to Lidar VFX and Plowman Craven Associates lidar surveys of the set, and 3D motion tracks of stereo plates generated at Yannix Technologies. "It was an immense amount of data," said Ben Grossmann. "At the end of each shoot day, we had a Maya file that showed the exact front and end position of each camera setup, lens orientation and all the camera equipment. Plus, for 90 percent of the shots, we had the camera data from Nvizage's MotionBuilder system where they had encoded camera moves, so we could see all the articulation of a crane arm or a dolly track, and the speed of travel. We then oriented motion control data to our Totalstation surveys, and kept track of how set extensions differed from one shot to the next. Giles Harding, the on-set data wrangler, did an amazing job of tracking the Pace camera systems, combining that with metadata from the encoder systems and set surveys. And then we had to build a crazy pipeline to process all of thati The opening shot featured about 500 extras on set. A hundred crowd members also took part in texture shoots that Pixomondo CG supervisor Adam Watkins used to enhance the station crowd. We mapped high-resolution, 360-degree Hasselblad photographs of background extras onto a Massive-generated crowd," said Watkins. "They were fully rigged with cloth simulations. Ben and Alex also shot extras on a treadmill, using four cameras in front of a greenscreen. We projected their textures onto geometry match-animated to the treadmill performances. That gave us a library of digital doubles based on real photography. We used those if Marty had a shot of principal performers against greenscreen 12 / 30 and needed to insert a woman putting on lipstick, a man checking his ticket, a porter

HUGO pushing a bunch of suitcases - we could drop them in, reorient them and place them in correct stereo space." Pixomondo asset lead Simon Britnell oversaw creation of digital station props, including CG trains based on scans and photographic textures of the full-scale train at Longcross. Pixomondo adjusted rendering parameters to generate 15 trains and composited a vast amount of environmental detail in stereo.iWe used a combination of three compositing approaches," noted Alex Henning. "The first approach was traditional, using elements of smoke or steam on cards that we could place far enough away from camera that we wouldn't sense intra-object depth. We almost never got away with that! Next, we had a library of generic CG elements generated in 3dsMax, Fume or Houdini. Those included smoke and steam simulations, falling snow and dust effects rendered with various interocular stereo separations. Quite often, the movement of the camera was so specific we had to custom render elements with holdout mattes and line them up in excruciating detaili The introduction to the station evolved in postproduction to include a prologue segment depicting mysterious clockwork mechanisms that then transition to the aerial shot of Paris. Industrial Light & Magic generated the three-shot sequence, which dovetailed into work underway at Pixomondo. iRob Legato asked us to create a clockwork mechanism of moving gears," stated ILM visual effects supervisor John Knoll. Render Unto Caesar BY JOE FORDHAM our months before the release of Rise of the Planet of the Apes, a teaser trailer appeared featuring an uncannily human adult chimpanzee - his head bowed, eyes fixed down as the camera moved around him, until his gaze swiveled upward with menacing intent. The chilling five-second shot depicted a different breed of ape than had been seen in previous Planet of the Apes films - a digital creation, not a prosthetic makeup - and ignited a firestorm of debate among aficionados of the franchise. To many monster movie fans, it seemed anathema that a new Apes film would abandon practical makeup effects. The 1968 original and four sequels inspired by Pierre Boulle's novel all had featured prosthetic makeups by John Chambers, who earned an honorary Oscar for his depictions of a civilization of talking apes. Creationisms BY JODY DUNCAN JESSER • t is not surprising that writer-director Terrence Malick spent several decades ruminating on The Tree of Life, for the film tackles the ultimate issues that have confronted humankind since its inception - the meaning of existence, faith, death, and the origins of life itself. Such ambitious themes demanded thoughtful consideration, and Malick gave them their due over the course of 30-plus years. The nonlinear narrative intercuts a modern-day story that follows Jack O'Brien (Sean Penn) as he suffers a crisis of the soul with flashbacks to his childhood growing up in 1950s small-town Texas under the watchful eye of an authoritarian father (Brad Pitt) and the gentle ministrations of a loving mother (Jessica Chastain). About a third of the way into the film, Malick offers up a breathtaking, 22-minute 'creation' sequence that begins with the Big Bang and then progresses through the formation of the universe and the evolution of life on earth. Realizing that the sequence would require visual effects expertise, artistry, and a willingness to let the work unfold in an organic, evolutionary manner over the course of sev1 / 22 eral years, Malick sought out visual effects supervisor Dan Glass, who first met with him

TREE OF LIFE in May 2006 to discuss the project. From that initial meeting, Malick - a newcomer to visual effects - stressed that he wanted to use as much photographic material as possible in the sequence. Even though he knew that we would have to enhance that material with CG effects," recalled Glass, "he wanted to incorporate imagery from the Hubble and other telescopes, IMAX plates and, eventually, practical elements that we shot ourselves. He understood that we'd need visual effects, but he also knew that the way visual effects are typically done doesn't fit the way he works. He shoots live-action almost improvisationally. He shoots very long takes, and he li purposely distract the actors so that he might capture an unplanned moment. Often, the bits of performance he prefers are those that happen after he has said 'cut' - that moment when the actor transitions from performing to being himself. He likes to capture that naturalness and lack of self-consciousness. "Terry was keen to achieve the same improvisational style with visual effects - but improvisation is anathema to visual effects. The great challenge of this project was to introduce an air of improvisation into the inherently deliberate and preplanned process of producing visual effects. Those effects would have to be manufactured as they always are, of course; but our job was to remove that sense of manufacture. After his initial meetings with Malick, Glass divided the creation sequence into three 'realms': the astrophysical realm, comprised of images representing the cosmic origins of the universe; the microbial realm involving microscopic biological organisms; and the natural history realm, which would illustrate key evolutionary stages of life on earth, with an emphasis on eras in which dinosaurs roamed the planet. Though Malick would take 2 / 22 some creative license in each realm, the entire sequence would be founded on sound

TREE OF LIFE scientific theory.Terry was obsessive about there being scientific fact and detail behind everything we were portraying," said Glass. "So each shot not only went through aesthetic evolutions, but it also went through constant vetting and referral back to science. A shot didn't have to be a literal representation of the science - Terry was more interested in its being an emotional representation - but it had to be grounded in science." alick and Glass brainstormed ideas for nearly two years; and by March 2008, M concepts take shape as previsualization. The filmmakers hired previz and digital effects supervisor Brad Friedman to oversee the previz assignment; but Friedman's first task, before producing a single animatic, was to gather the many notes, images, scientific data and other research materials Malick had been accumulating for decades and organize them in a digital library system. There was footage that had been shot in the Seventies," Friedman recalled, "and notes that came from the same period. There were recorded pieces of music, and boxes and boxes of research materials. Terry had been thinking about this project in one form or another for 30 years; and throughout that period, he'd been accumulating anything he thought might be useful. Friedman organized the material in a Filemaker database, and then started assigning key pieces of reference to specific shots in the sequence. "We related the materials to the script," related Friedman, "referencing it to scene numbers. That process rolled very naturally into previz - but a different type of previz than what we normally do. On most 3 / 22 films, you open up a 3D package and start with storyboards and shot lists. This was more

an editorial process of starting with the bits of music, notes and images that Terry had collected, putting them into some form that related to the chronology of the sequence, and then jumping off from those materials to create shots in previz that Terry could react to." As the previz assignment gained traction, Dan Glass brought on five visual effects artists to join Friedman in Austin, setting up workspace next to Malick's editorial offices. "It was especially important to be close to Terry and get his input," explained Glass, "because we knew we'd be doing a lot of exploration and experimentation. It was going to be a very organic, evolutionary process; and that meant we had to have Terry there to react to things on a regular basis." filmmaker and effects pioneer Douglas Trumbull had first investigated during his tenure on Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey 40 years earlier.
